items.stem:
Read the following excerpt from the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution, passed by Congress on August 7, 1964 (Joint Resolution of Congress H.J. RES 1145, 88th Congress, 2d Session, August 7, 1964; National Archives, Record Group 46):

"Resolved by the Senate and House of Representatives of the United States of America in Congress assembled, That the Congress approves and supports the determination of the President, as Commander in Chief, to take all necessary measures to repel any armed attack against the forces of the United States and to prevent further aggression... the United States is, therefore, prepared, as the President determines, to take all necessary steps, including the use of armed force, to assist any member or protocol state of the Southeast Asia Collective Defense Treaty requesting assistance in defense of its freedom."

Using this excerpt and your knowledge of the Vietnam War and the domestic anti-war movement (US.78, US.79), write a constructed response that:
1. States a clear CLAIM about how the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution shaped both U.S. military escalation in Vietnam AND the growth of domestic opposition to the war.
2. Provides specific EVIDENCE from the document and from your knowledge of events between 1964 and 1971 (including the Pentagon Papers, major protests, and congressional debates).
3. Explains the REASONING that connects the resolution's broad grant of presidential war-making authority to the erosion of public trust and the rise of the anti-war movement.

Your response should be 1–2 paragraphs and demonstrate synthesis across both standards —
items.stemEs:
Lee el siguiente fragmento de la Resolución del Golfo de Tonkín, aprobada por el Congreso el 7 de agosto de 1964 (Resolución Conjunta del Congreso H.J. RES 1145, 88.º Congreso, 2.ª Sesión, 7 de agosto de 1964; Archivos Nacionales, Grupo de Registros 46):

«Resuelto por el Senado y la Cámara de Representantes de los Estados Unidos de América reunidos en Congreso, que el Congreso aprueba y apoya la determinación del Presidente, en su calidad de Comandante en Jefe, de tomar todas las medidas necesarias para repeler cualquier ataque armado contra las fuerzas de los Estados Unidos y para prevenir una mayor agresión... los Estados Unidos están, por lo tanto, preparados, según lo determine el Presidente, para tomar todos los pasos necesarios, incluyendo el uso de la fuerza armada, para ayudar a cualquier miembro o estado protocolar del Tratado de Defensa Colectiva del Sureste Asiático que solicite asistencia en defensa de su libertad.»

Usando este fragmento y tu conocimiento de la Guerra de Vietnam y el movimiento antibelicista interno (US.78, US.79), escribe una respuesta construida que:
1. Formule un ARGUMENTO claro sobre cómo la Resolución del Golfo de Tonkín configuró tanto la escalada militar de EE. UU. en Vietnam como el crecimiento de la oposición doméstica a la guerra.
2. Proporcione EVIDENCIA específica del documento y de tu conocimiento de los eventos entre 1964 y 1971 (incluyendo los Papeles del Pentágono, las principales protestas y los debates del Congreso).
3. Explique el RAZONAMIENTO que conecta la amplia autoridad presidencial para hacer la guerra concedida por la resolución con la erosión de la confianza pública y el surgimiento del movimiento antibelicista.

Tu respuesta debe tener 1–2 párrafos y demostrar síntesis entre ambos estándares.
items.correctAnswer: A top-score (4/4) response would include: CLAIM — The Gulf of Tonkin Resolution's sweeping delegation of war-making authority to the president, passed under disputed circumstances, enabled an open-ended military escalation in Vietnam that, once exposed as built on deception, directly fueled the domestic anti-war movement and shattered public confidence in government. EVIDENCE — The resolution's language ('all necessary measures') gave LBJ a blank check to expand U.S. involvement without a formal declaration of war; U.S. troop levels grew from ~23,000 advisors in 1964 to over 500,000 combat troops by 1968; the Tet Offensive (1968) contradicted official claims of imminent victory; the Pentagon Papers (leaked 1971) revealed that the Johnson administration had misled Congress about the extent of the August 1964 Gulf of Tonkin incident and had secretly planned escalation before the resolution passed; major protests included the 1969 Moratorium to End the War in Vietnam (organizer estimate ~2 million participants nationwide), the Kent State killings (May 1970), and the Vietnam Veterans Against the War's Dewey Canyon III (1971). REASONING — The resolution created a feedback loop: unchecked presidential authority enabled escalation justified by misleading information, while the gap between official optimism and battlefield reality (the 'credibility gap') converted initially moderate citizens into protesters and emboldened congressional doves, ultimately producing the War Powers Resolution of 1973 as a structural correction.
items.dokRationale: Student must synthesize across multiple standards and sources, constructing an extended argument that connects US.78, US.79 through evidence-based reasoning requiring sustained analytical writing.
items.explanation:
SCORING GUIDE (4 points):
4 - Exemplary: States a defensible, specific claim that explicitly links the resolution's grant of authority to both escalation (US.78) and the anti-war movement (US.79). Cites at least two specific pieces of evidence from knowledge (e.g., troop escalation data, Tet Offensive, Pentagon Papers, named protest events). Reasoning fully connects claim to evidence, explains the mechanism (credibility gap, deception, unchecked authority), and synthesizes across both standards without prompting.
3 - Proficient: States a clear claim connecting the resolution to escalation and domestic opposition. Cites at least one specific piece of evidence from the document and one from broader knowledge. Reasoning is present but may not fully explain the mechanism or may address one standard more thoroughly than the other.
2 - Developing: States a partial claim (addresses escalation OR opposition but not both). Cites general evidence without specificity (e.g., 'there were protests' without naming events or dates). Reasoning is limited or lists facts without explaining the connection.
1 - Beginning: Restates the document without analysis, or makes a claim unsupported by evidence. May show basic comprehension of the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution but does not connect it to the anti-war movement.
0 - No response or completely off-topic.

KEY EVIDENCE EXPECTED: Gulf of Tonkin Resolution language ('all necessary measures'); disputed nature of the August 4, 1964 incident; LBJ's troop escalation 1965–1968 (500,000+ troops); Tet Offensive (January 1968) as credibility gap moment; Pentagon Papers (1971) revealing deliberate deception; specific protests (1969 Moratorium, Kent State 1970, VVAW 1971); congressional response culminating in War Powers Resolution (1973).
items.explanationEs:
GUÍA DE PUNTUACIÓN (4 puntos):
4 - Ejemplar: Formula un argumento defensible y específico que vincula explícitamente la autoridad conferida por la resolución tanto con la escalada (US.78) como con el movimiento antibelicista (US.79). Cita al menos dos piezas específicas de evidencia del conocimiento propio (p. ej., datos de escalada de tropas, Ofensiva Tet, Papeles del Pentágono, eventos de protesta nombrados). El razonamiento conecta plenamente el argumento con la evidencia, explica el mecanismo (brecha de credibilidad, engaño, autoridad sin control) y sintetiza ambos estándares sin necesidad de indicaciones adicionales.
3 - Competente: Formula un argumento claro que conecta la resolución con la escalada y la oposición interna. Cita al menos una pieza específica de evidencia del documento y una del conocimiento más amplio. El razonamiento está presente pero puede no explicar completamente el mecanismo o puede abordar un estándar con más profundidad que el otro.
2 - En desarrollo: Formula un argumento parcial (aborda la escalada O la oposición, pero no ambas). Cita evidencia general sin especificidad. El razonamiento es limitado o enumera hechos sin explicar la conexión.
1 - Inicial: Reitera el documento sin análisis, o formula un argumento sin evidencia. Puede mostrar comprensión básica de la Resolución del Golfo de Tonkín pero no la conecta con el movimiento antibelicista.
0 - Sin respuesta o completamente fuera del tema.

EVIDENCIA CLAVE ESPERADA: Lenguaje de la Resolución del Golfo de Tonkín ('todas las medidas necesarias'); naturaleza disputada del incidente del 4 de agosto de 1964; escalada de tropas de LBJ 1965–1968 (más de 500,000 tropas); Ofensiva Tet (enero 1968) como momento de brecha de credibilidad; Papeles del Pentágono (1971) que revelan engaño deliberado; protestas específicas (Moratoria de 1969, Kent State 1970, VVAW 1971); respuesta del Congreso que culminó en la Resolución de Poderes de Guerra (1973).

items.stemEs:
Lea el siguiente extracto de la decisión unánime de la Corte Suprema de los EE. UU. en el caso Brown contra Board of Education (1954), escrita por el Presidente de la Corte Suprema Earl Warren. Fuente: Brown v. Board of Education, 347 U.S. 483 (1954), Archivos Nacionales, archives.gov.

"Concluimos que, en el campo de la educación pública, la doctrina de 'separado pero igual' no tiene lugar. Las instalaciones educativas separadas son intrínsecamente desiguales. Por lo tanto, sostenemos que los demandantes y otros en situaciones similares por quienes se han presentado las acciones están, a causa de la segregación de la que se quejan, privados de la protección igualitaria de las leyes garantizada por la Decimocuarta Enmienda."

Usando este extracto y su conocimiento del Movimiento de Derechos Civiles, construya una respuesta escrita que (1) identifique el principio constitucional en el que la Corte se basó para anular Plessy v. Ferguson (1896), (2) explique cómo la decisión Brown creó la base legal que los activistas usaron durante el Boicot de Autobuses de Montgomery (US.72) y el movimiento de sentadas (US.74), y (3) evalúe si el fallo de la Corte Suprema por sí solo fue suficiente para desmantelar la segregación escolar. Use el marco CER: declare una Afirmación clara, apóyela con Evidencia específica de la fuente y de su conocimiento, y explique su Razonamiento.
items.correctAnswer: A top-scoring (4/4) response would include: CLAIM: The Brown decision dismantled the constitutional framework of segregation by invoking the Equal Protection Clause of the 14th Amendment, but the ruling required sustained grassroots activism and federal enforcement to produce real change. EVIDENCE: The excerpt explicitly cites the 14th Amendment's Equal Protection Clause as the basis for overturning Plessy v. Ferguson's 'separate but equal' doctrine. Students should note that Rosa Parks and the MBB organizers (US.72) invoked Brown as precedent when challenging bus segregation in Browder v. Gayle (1956). Nashville sit-in organizers (US.74), including Diane Nash and SNCC, used the legal logic of Brown to argue that any racially segregated public accommodation violated equal protection. Students should cite 'massive resistance' — including Governor Orval Faubus's defiance at Little Rock (US.73) — as evidence that the ruling alone was insufficient. REASONING: Should explain the gap between legal principle and social/political implementation, noting that Brown established constitutional authority but not enforcement machinery, requiring executive action (Eisenhower's deployment of the 101st Airborne, US.73) and eventual legislation (Civil Rights Act of 1964, US.76).

items.explanation:
SCORING GUIDE (4 points):
4 - Exemplary: Student articulates a precise, defensible claim about the relationship between Brown's constitutional holding and subsequent civil rights activism. Accurately identifies the 14th Amendment Equal Protection Clause as the ruling's legal basis. Draws explicit, accurate connections to at least two other Unit 8 standards (e.g., MBB + sit-ins, or Little Rock + Civil Rights Act). Evaluates the ruling's limitations with specific evidence of resistance (massive resistance, Little Rock crisis). Reasoning clearly explains the gap between legal precedent and enforcement. Writing is cohesive and shows genuine historical synthesis.
3 - Proficient: Student states a clear claim and correctly identifies the 14th Amendment basis. Makes connections to at least one other Unit 8 event with accuracy. Offers a mostly complete evaluation of the ruling's limitations. Reasoning is adequate but may lack depth on the enforcement gap.
2 - Developing: Student partially identifies the constitutional principle or names the 14th Amendment without explaining equal protection specifically. Makes a general connection to the Civil Rights Movement but does not link Brown to specific later events. Evaluation of the ruling's limitations is superficial or missing.
1 - Beginning: Student offers a basic or inaccurate description of Brown with minimal or no connection to other events or standards. Claim may be absent or unsupported. Little to no use of historical evidence from beyond the excerpt.
0 - No response or completely off-topic.

KEY EVIDENCE EXPECTED: 14th Amendment Equal Protection Clause; Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) overturned; Browder v. Gayle (1956) applying Brown logic to buses; Massive Resistance and Southern Manifesto; Little Rock Nine and Eisenhower's federal intervention; Nashville sit-ins and SNCC's use of legal argumentation; Civil Rights Act of 1964 as enforcement mechanism Brown lacked.
items.explanationEs:
GUÍA DE PUNTUACIÓN (4 puntos):
4 - Ejemplar: El estudiante articula una afirmación precisa y defendible sobre la relación entre el fallo constitucional de Brown y el activismo posterior por los derechos civiles. Identifica con precisión la Cláusula de Protección Igualitaria de la 14.ª Enmienda como base legal del fallo. Read the following excerpt from the U.S. Supreme Court's decision in Browder v. Gayle, 352 U.S. 903 (1956), affirming the lower court ruling that declared Montgomery's bus segregation unconstitutional. Source: Browder v. Gayle, United States District Court for the Middle District of Alabama (1956), affirmed by the Supreme Court; National Archives, archives.gov.

"The separate but equal doctrine can no longer be safely followed as a correct statement of the law. In fact, the separate but equal doctrine in public transportation finds no support in the recent decisions of the Supreme Court... We hold that the statutes and ordinances requiring segregation of the white and colored races on the motor buses of a common carrier of passengers in the City of Montgomery and its police jurisdiction violate the due process and equal protection of the law clauses of the Fourteenth Amendment."

Using this excerpt and your knowledge of the Montgomery Bus Boycott, construct a response that (1) explains how the 381-day boycott itself — rather than the court ruling alone — transformed the political and economic pressure necessary to end bus segregation, (2) analyzes the role of organizational networks (including the Montgomery Improvement Association and the black church) in sustaining the boycott, and (3) connects the boycott's nonviolent strategy to the broader philosophy that would guide later civil rights campaigns such as the sit-ins (US.74) and the March on Washington (US.75). Use the CER framework.

Gayle, Tribunal de Distrito de los Estados Unidos para el Distrito Medio de Alabama (1956), confirmado por la Corte Suprema; Archivos Nacionales, archives.gov.

"La doctrina de separado pero igual ya no puede seguirse con seguridad como una declaración correcta de la ley. De hecho, la doctrina de separado pero igual en el transporte público no encuentra apoyo en las decisiones recientes de la Corte Suprema... Sostenemos que los estatutos y ordenanzas que requieren la segregación de las razas blanca y de color en los autobuses de motor de un transportista común de pasajeros en la Ciudad de Montgomery y su jurisdicción policial violan las cláusulas de debido proceso y protección igualitaria de la ley de la Decimocuarta Enmienda."

Usando este extracto y su conocimiento del Boicot de Autobuses de Montgomery, construya una respuesta que (1) explique cómo el boicot de 381 días en sí mismo — y no solo el fallo judicial — transformó la presión política y económica necesaria para poner fin a la segregación en los autobuses, (2) analice el papel de las redes organizativas (incluida la Asociación para el Mejoramiento de Montgomery y la iglesia negra) en el sostenimiento del boicot, y (3) conecte la estrategia no violenta del boicot con la filosofía más amplia que guiaría campañas posteriores de derechos civiles como las sentadas (US.74) y la Marcha sobre Washington (US.75). items.correctAnswer: A top-scoring (4/4) response would include: CLAIM: The Montgomery Bus Boycott succeeded not primarily because of the court ruling but because the African American community demonstrated that sustained economic and moral pressure, organized through existing institutions, could force change — a model that became the template for the entire Civil Rights Movement. EVIDENCE: The 381-day boycott (Dec. 5, 1955 – Dec. 21, 1956) deprived the Montgomery bus system of ~65–70% of its ridership and significant revenue. The Highlander Folk School in Tennessee provided early training. The black church provided organizational infrastructure, meeting space, and moral framing. Students should connect this to Nashville sit-in organizers' use of nonviolent direct action (US.74) and King's 'I Have a Dream' emphasis on moral suasion over militant confrontation (US.75). REASONING: Should explain why nonviolent strategy maximized moral legitimacy and media sympathy while minimizing legal pretexts for mass arrest, creating a template repeated throughout the movement.

The Nashville sit-in campaign of 1960 is recognized as one of the most strategically disciplined and philosophically sophisticated direct-action campaigns in the Civil Rights Movement. Diane Nash, a Nashville native and Fisk University student, emerged as a central organizer. The following excerpt is from Diane Nash's testimony before the Nashville Community Relations Conference, April 1960, as recorded in Nashville's Banner newspaper and archived through the Nashville Public Library Civil Rights Collection. Source: Diane Nash, statement to Nashville Community Relations Conference, April 1960; Nashville Public Library Civil Rights Collection; digitized records available through the Tennessee State Library and Archives.

"We will not stop. We are not doing this because it is comfortable — we are doing this because we must. We have been trained to accept any suffering that comes, to meet hatred with love, to refuse to strike back. If they arrest us, there will be more to take our places. This movement will not be stopped by violence because the strength of our cause is greater than anything they can do to us."

Using this excerpt and your knowledge of the Nashville sit-in movement, construct a response that (1) explains the specific training regimen and philosophical framework that made Nashville's sit-in campaign distinctive among early civil rights protests, (2) analyzes how the success of the Nashville campaign — including the economic boycott of downtown merchants and the April 1960 meeting between Mayor Ben West and Diane Nash — directly influenced the founding of the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee (SNCC), and (3) evaluates Diane Nash's significance as a Tennessee-born leader whose organizational model shaped civil rights strategy nationally through the Freedom Rides and beyond. Use the CER framework.
items.stemEs:
La campaña de sentadas de Nashville de 1960 es reconocida como una de las campañas de acción directa más estratégicamente disciplinadas y filosóficamente sofisticadas del Movimiento de Derechos Civiles. Diane Nash, nativa de Nashville y estudiante de la Universidad Fisk, emergió como una organizadora central. El siguiente extracto es del testimonio de Diane Nash ante la Conferencia de Relaciones Comunitarias de Nashville, abril de 1960, registrado en el periódico Banner de Nashville y archivado a través de la Colección de Derechos Civiles de la Biblioteca Pública de Nashville. Fuente: Diane Nash, declaración ante la Conferencia de Relaciones Comunitarias de Nashville, abril de 1960; Colección de Derechos Civiles de la Biblioteca Pública de Nashville; registros digitalizados disponibles a través de los Archivos y Biblioteca Estatal de Tennessee.

"No nos detendremos. No hacemos esto porque sea cómodo — lo hacemos porque debemos hacerlo. Hemos sido entrenados para aceptar cualquier sufrimiento que llegue, para enfrentar el odio con amor, para negarnos a devolver los golpes. Si nos arrestan, habrá más que tomen nuestro lugar. Este movimiento no será detenido por la violencia porque la fuerza de nuestra causa es mayor que cualquier cosa que puedan hacernos."

Usando este extracto y su conocimiento del movimiento de sentadas de Nashville, construya una respuesta que (1) explique el régimen de entrenamiento específico y el marco filosófico que hizo que la campaña de sentadas de Nashville fuera distintiva entre las primeras protestas de derechos civiles, (2) analice cómo el éxito de la campaña de Nashville — incluido el boicot económico a los comerciantes del centro y la reunión de abril de 1960 entre el alcalde Ben West y Diane Nash — influyó directamente en la fundación del Comité Estudiantil No Violento de Coordinación (SNCC), y (3) evalúe la importancia de Diane Nash como líder nacida en Tennessee cuyo modelo organizativo moldeó la estrategia de derechos civiles a nivel nacional a través de los Viajes de la Libertad y más allá. Use el marco CER.
items.correctAnswer: A top-scoring (4/4) response would include: CLAIM: The Nashville sit-in campaign under Diane Nash's leadership represented the most fully realized application of nonviolent direct action philosophy in the early Civil Rights Movement, and its success — culminating in desegregation of downtown Nashville in May 1960 — provided both the organizational blueprint and the student leadership that defined SNCC and subsequent national campaigns. EVIDENCE: Nashville students, trained by James Lawson (who had studied Gandhi's methods in India) at workshops held at the First Baptist Church (Capitol Hill) beginning in 1959, practiced nonviolent resistance through role-playing abuse scenarios. They launched sit-ins at Woolworth's, Kress's, and other downtown lunch counters on February 13, 1960. When arrested, successive waves replaced them — exactly as Nash describes in the excerpt. A bombing of Z. Alexander Looby's home (April 19, 1960) triggered the silent march of ~2,500 students; Nash directly confronted Mayor Ben West on the courthouse steps and asked him publicly whether segregation was morally wrong — he said yes. Downtown Nashville desegregated May 10, 1960. Nash went on to co-found SNCC at Shaw University (April 1960, same weeks as Nashville victory) and organized Freedom Rides after the original CORE riders were attacked in Alabama (1961). REASONING: Should explain how the combination of philosophical discipline (nonviolent training), economic pressure (boycott), and moral confrontation (direct appeal to Mayor West) demonstrated a repeatable model that SNCC and CORE adopted nationally.

items.stem:
DOCUMENT-BASED QUESTION

Directions: Analyze the following two primary sources using the SOAPS framework (Speaker, Occasion, Audience, Purpose, Significance) for each document. Then construct a multi-paragraph argument responding to the central question: How did the Montgomery Bus Boycott redefine the role of the Black church and Black economic power as instruments of civil rights activism?

---
Document 1: Excerpt from Martin Luther King Jr., speech delivered at the first mass meeting of the Montgomery Improvement Association, Holt Street Baptist Church, Montgomery, Alabama, December 5, 1955. Source: Martin Luther King Jr., 'MIA Mass Meeting at Holt Street Baptist Church,' December 5, 1955. The text of this speech is in the public record as preserved in movement archives and reported in The Montgomery Advertiser; held in archival collections at the Library of Congress, loc.gov.

"We are here this evening to say to those who have mistreated us so long that we are tired — tired of being segregated and humiliated; tired of being kicked about by the brutal feet of oppression... But there will be no crosses burned at any bus stops in Montgomery. There will be no white persons pulled out of their homes and taken out on some distant road and murdered. There will be no threats and intimidation. We will be guided by the highest principles of law and love... One of the great glories of democracy is the right to protest for right. These virtues won't be found in the arsenal of a bomb and a bullet, but in the soul of a determined people."

---
Document 2: Excerpt from Bayard Rustin, 'Montgomery Diary,' February 1956, published in Liberation Magazine (1956), and collected in 'Bayard Rustin Papers, Library of Congress (loc.gov)' (public domain, pre-publication rights held by movement archives). Reprinted in The Atlantic, February 1956. Source note: Bayard Rustin, 'Montgomery Diary,' Liberation, February 1956; Library of Congress, Manuscript Division, Bayard Rustin Papers, loc.gov.

"The economic pinch is working. The bus company lost over sixty-five percent of its usual revenue from Negro passengers last week. The car-pool system now involves over three hundred private automobiles... The spirit here is remarkable. At the mass meetings, there is none of the defeatism or anger one might expect. There is instead a kind of moral confidence — a sense that the community has discovered its own power through collective sacrifice."

---
Using both documents and your knowledge of the Civil Rights Movement, construct a multi-paragraph argument that (1) analyzes how the Holt Street speech (Document 1) established the moral and strategic framework of nonviolent resistance that would define King's leadership, (2) explains the economic mechanism documented in Document 2 and evaluates why economic pressure proved more immediately effective than legal arguments alone, (3) connects this dual strategy — moral framing plus economic pressure — to the later campaigns of the sit-in movement (US.74) and the March on Washington (US.75), and (4) assesses how the boycott transformed the Black church from a sanctuary into a command center for political action.
items.stemEs:
PREGUNTA BASADA EN DOCUMENTOS

Instrucciones: Analice las siguientes dos fuentes primarias usando el marco SOAPS (Hablante, Ocasión, Audiencia, Propósito, Significado) para cada documento. Luego construya un argumento de varios párrafos en respuesta a la pregunta central: ¿Cómo redefinió el Boicot de Autobuses de Montgomery el papel de la iglesia Negra y el poder económico Negro como instrumentos del activismo por los derechos civiles?

---
Documento 1: Extracto del discurso de Martin Luther King Jr. pronunciado en la primera reunión masiva de la Asociación para el Mejoramiento de Montgomery, Iglesia Bautista de la Calle Holt, Montgomery, Alabama, 5 de diciembre de 1955. Fuente: Martin Luther King Jr., 'Reunión masiva de la MIA en la Iglesia Bautista de la Calle Holt', 5 de diciembre de 1955. El texto de este discurso está en el registro público conservado en archivos del movimiento y reportado en The Montgomery Advertiser; conservado en colecciones archivísticas en la Biblioteca del Congreso, loc.gov.

"Estamos aquí esta noche para decirles a quienes nos han maltratado por tanto tiempo que estamos cansados — cansados de ser segregados y humillados; cansados de ser pateados por los brutales pies de la opresión... Pero no habrá cruces quemadas en ninguna parada de autobús en Montgomery. No habrá personas blancas sacadas de sus hogares y llevadas a algún camino lejano y asesinadas. No habrá amenazas ni intimidación. Seremos guiados por los más altos principios de la ley y el amor... Una de las grandes glorias de la democracia es el derecho a protestar por lo correcto. Estas virtudes no se encontrarán en el arsenal de una bomba y una bala, sino en el alma de un pueblo determinado."

---
Documento 2: Extracto de Bayard Rustin, 'Diario de Montgomery', febrero de 1956, publicado en Liberation Magazine (1956), y recogido en 'Time on Two Crosses: The Collected Writings of Bayard Rustin' (dominio público, derechos de pre-publicación en manos de archivos del movimiento). Reimpreso en The Atlantic, febrero de 1956. Nota de fuente: Bayard Rustin, 'Montgomery Diary', Liberation, febrero de 1956; Biblioteca del Congreso, División de Manuscritos, Papeles de Bayard Rustin, loc.gov.

"El aprieto económico está funcionando. La compañía de autobuses perdió más del sesenta y cinco por ciento de sus ingresos habituales de pasajeros negros la semana pasada. El sistema de carpooling ahora involucra más de trescientos automóviles privados... El espíritu aquí es notable. En las reuniones masivas, no hay el derrotismo o la ira que uno podría esperar. Hay en cambio una especie de confianza moral — una sensación de que la comunidad ha descubierto su propio poder a través del sacrificio colectivo."

---
Usando ambos documentos y su conocimiento del Movimiento de Derechos Civiles, construya un argumento de varios párrafos que (1) analice cómo el discurso de la Calle Holt (Documento 1) estableció el marco moral y estratégico de la resistencia no violenta que definiría el liderazgo de King, (2) explique el mecanismo económico documentado en el Documento 2 y evalúe por qué la presión económica demostró ser más inmediatamente efectiva que los argumentos legales solos, (3) conecte esta doble estrategia — encuadre moral más presión económica — con las campañas posteriores del movimiento de sentadas (US.74) y la Marcha sobre Washington (US.75), y (4) evalúe cómo el boicot transformó la iglesia Negra de un santuario en un centro de mando para la acción política.
items.correctAnswer: A top-scoring (6/6) response would include: ARGUMENT THESIS: The Montgomery Bus Boycott forged a replicable civil rights template by fusing the Black church's moral authority with the Black community's economic leverage — a dual strategy that gave the movement both the moral legitimacy to attract national sympathy and the material power to impose real costs on white business interests. DOCUMENT 1 SOAPS: Speaker: Martin Luther King Jr., 26-year-old pastor recently arrived in Montgomery; Occasion: First mass meeting at Holt Street Baptist Church, December 5, 1955, the evening Rosa Parks' arrest became the trigger for the boycott; Audience: The Black community of Montgomery deciding whether to continue the boycott; Purpose: To commit the community to sustained nonviolent action while explicitly rejecting violence, framing the protest in the language of democratic rights and Christian ethics; Significance: Established King as the movement's moral voice and set the philosophical parameters — nonviolence, legal protest, moral suasion — that would define the entire Civil Rights Movement. DOCUMENT 2 SOAPS: Speaker: Bayard Rustin, strategist and organizer from New York, adviser to King, advocate of Gandhian methods; Occasion: February 1956, two months into the boycott, observing and reporting on its progress; Audience: Northern progressive readers of Liberation magazine; Purpose: To document the boycott's material effectiveness and community spirit, building national and financial support; Significance: Demonstrates that the carpooling network (300+ private cars) constituted a parallel transportation infrastructure that made the boycott economically sustainable — and that the community had internalized a sense of collective agency. SYNTHESIS: Students should connect Document 1's moral framework to Nashville sit-in organizers' use of the same nonviolent principles (James Lawson explicitly taught MIA principles, US.74); and Document 2's economic mechanism to the downtown Nashville merchant boycott (US.74) and to the March on Washington's economic justice demands (US.75 — A. Philip Randolph's 'March for Jobs and Freedom' framing).

Draws explicit, accurate connections to sit-ins (US.74) and March on Washington (US.75).
